To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
thermal spreading and heat conduction during laser heating are poor in advanced interconnect schemes, making defect localization difficult in multi-level metallization structures.

the laser-based defect localization technique is most effective in the first few levels of metal, and the technique is less effective in the newer interconnection schemes with copper and low-k materials.
the thermal distribution and spreading during laser heating are affected more by interconnect geometrical factors than by variations in the laser spot size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a fundamental understanding of laser-based techniques for defect localization in advanced interconnect structures.
the development and validation of a thermal model that can be used to predict the effectiveness of laser heating for defect detection in advanced interconnect structures.
developing a better understanding of laser heating of advanced multi-level interconnect systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
localized laser heating is not a viable technique for defect detection in advanced metallization structures with more than three levels of metal.
localized laser heating is not an effective means of defect detection in advanced interconnect schemes.
localized laser heating is not effective in detecting defects in advanced interconnect schemes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
thermal modeling can be used to predict thermal profiles in interconnect systems with complex metallization structures.
localized laser heating is effective in defect detection only in the first few levels of metal.

laser-based techniques for defect detection are effective only for the top three levels of interconnects in state-of-the art metallization schemes and that the newer materials used in advanced inter-connection systems are less effective than conventional materials for laser-based defect detection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the thermal distribution from the laser is very sensitive to the interconnect geometry and material system and that the thermal distribution is very different for advanced interconnects than for conventional metallization schemes.
the effectiveness of laser techniques in detecting defects in advanced interconnects depends strongly on the metallization complexity and material properties.
the thermal spreading during laser-induced defect detection is more important than the temperature rise in determining the effectiveness of the technique in defect localization.
